text:
To answer any query, the database first has to find the data. If there's no index, it does a full scan: it reads every row in the table in order until it reaches the ones you asked for. You won't notice this on a small table. On a large table, it's why your dashboard keeps loading and your users give up and leave.

A database index is similar to the index at the back of a textbook. It's a separate structure, kept in sorted order and usually built as a B-tree, that maps the values you search on to the locations of the matching rows. A B-tree stays balanced and has many branches at each level, so a lookup takes O(log n) steps rather than n. A table can have millions of rows and the database will still reach the right one after visiting only a few nodes.

The speedup can be dramatic. In one case, a query on a 10-million-row table ran in 2.1 seconds without an index and 4 milliseconds with the right one.

There is a cost. Every insert, update, and delete also has to update the index, and in that same case writes got about 15% slower. Most of the skill in indexing is knowing when that cost is worth paying.
